answer:
The distribution of RNA expression data is HIGHLY RIGHT-SKEWED.

Supporting statistics (data as supplied, linear scale):
- Pooled Fisher–Pearson skewness G1 = 42.44 over all 6,724,656 gene×sample values — enormous relative to the ~0.0009 SE under normality (≈45,000 SEs); D'Agostino K² = 3.03×10⁶ and Jarque–Bera = 1.07×10¹² (both p ≈ 0) decisively reject normality.
- Corroborating measures agree in sign and magnitude: Pearson-2 skewness = +0.57 (mean 931.96 ≫ median 176.79) and Bowley quantile skewness = +0.575 on a −1…+1 scale (well toward the extreme-right pole).
- Shape: a spike of exact zeros (15.2% of values) at the left edge, a dense right-leaning body (median 177, Q3 819, 99th pct ~10,900) and a thin tail stretching to 1.34 million; a normal fit with the same mean/SD would predict negative values and grossly understate the upper tail (QQ view: observed values collapse to 0 where the normal expects −15,299).
- Per-sample: all 328 samples have positive skewness (median G1 = 20.6, IQR 17.9–26.5, range 11.5–110.8). Per-gene: 97.5% of genes have positive skewness across samples (median G1 = 1.98).
- Sensitivities: tumor-only (285 primary-tumor samples) G1 = 36.0 — same verdict; averaging the 34 duplicated gene symbols changes G1 negligibly (42.44 → 42.42) — no effect on any conclusion.
- Clearly-labeled scale sensitivity: on log2(x+1) values, pooled G1 = −0.30 (slightly left-skewed due to the 15% zero atom; still far from normal, p ≈ 0). The final verdict is based on the data as supplied (raw, linear-scale RSEM counts), which are highly right-skewed.

Concise answer: The RNA expression data are highly right-skewed — the pooled distribution has Fisher–Pearson skewness ≈ 42 (vs. 0 for normal; mean 932 ≫ median 177), every sample and ~98% of genes show positive skew, and normality is decisively rejected.
